strengths: Well-motivated noise reduction framing for reranking with clear visual evidence of the problem (Figure 1)
Sound theoretical analysis of direct optimization limitations (Section 3.2) and variational framework derivation
Comprehensive experimental validation across three datasets with extensive ablations (RQ1-RQ6), sensitivity analysis, and online A/B testing showing 1.089% improvement on 100M+ users
Empirical justification for design choices (e.g., Beta vs. Gaussian noise comparison with distribution visualization)
Consistent improvements over strong state-of-the-art baselines including recent generator-evaluator and diffusion methods
Clear problem motivation and systematic research question structure
weaknesses: Key design choices lack rigorous justification: (1) noise injection formula Eq. 4 is ad-hoc without exploring alternatives, (2) Beta distribution choice is intuitive but not theoretically derived from Bernoulli feedback, (3) Eq. 8 approximation replacing KL with log ratio lacks error analysis
Theoretical predictions not empirically validated: magnitudes of L₁ and L₂ error terms not quantified, convergence of learned posterior pϕ to ground truth p_{x|z} not analyzed

Complex training procedure (Algorithm 1) with multi-phase approach switching samplers at epoch λ_e lacks clear justification; three hyperparameters (λc, λm, λe) show dataset-dependent sensitivity without principled tuning guidelines
Improvements over strong baselines sometimes modest (3-5% relative, e.g., ML-1M H@6: 64.89 vs Pier 62.74); ablation study (Table 3) shows varying magnitudes of component contributions across datasets
Reproducibility concerns: posterior architecture ϕ not clearly specified, 'true noise' computation in Figure 5 undefined, actual training cost multiplier not quantified, no code provided
Limited guidance on when DNR is beneficial; online A/B test on different task (PCTR prediction vs offline feedback labels) with unclear translation
Experimental scope limitations: fixed retriever prevents joint optimization, unobserved item assumption not validated, missing comparisons with simpler noise-aware baselines and recent 2024 methods

strengths: Novel perspective: Formulating reranking as a noise reduction problem is intuitive and well-motivated with convincing empirical evidence (Figure 1)
Solid theoretical analysis: Section 3.2 clearly identifies limitations of naive approaches (Ldirect) and the uncontrolled terms L1 and L2
Comprehensive experimental validation: Three public datasets + industrial A/B test with 100M+ users, diverse baselines, extensive ablations, and generalization studies
Consistent empirical improvements: 2-5% relative gains across all metrics and datasets; +1.089% improvement in real-world deployment
Strong reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, promised code release, experimental settings in appendices, online evaluation provided
weaknesses: Theoretical gaps: The solution (Eq. 5) doesn't directly address the identified problems (Eq. 3). No rigorous justification that optimizing Lz, Ladv, Lx brings pϕ closer to unknown px|z
Limited technical novelty: Three losses derived from standard VAE-like decomposition; 2-layer MLP generator; adversarial learning and data augmentation are well-established
Modest improvements over simpler baselines: Table 2 shows simple 'c score' concatenation achieves 76.73, DNR only 77.12 NDCG@6—0.39 point difference undermines necessity of complexity
Design choices lack principled justification: Linear interpolation in Eq. 4, ad-hoc epoch switching for noise generator, three hyperparameters requiring tuning
Online A/B test shows trade-offs: While realshow improves (+1.089%), watch-time and share-rate decrease; only 2 metrics are statistically significant
Scope limitations: Only binary implicit feedback; extension to ratings/multi-class unclear; multi-task scenarios deferred to future work
Approximation quality unvalidated: The approximation of Ladv in Eq. 7 is loose; no empirical evidence that learned pϕ approaches px|z

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation with compelling empirical evidence that retriever scores contain useful information and reranking acts as noise reduction (Figure 1 visualizations are particularly effective)
Principled theoretical grounding through variational inference framework; analytical decomposition (Eq. 3) clearly shows limitations of naive score incorporation
Comprehensive experimental validation including offline experiments on 3 datasets, online A/B testing on industrial platform with 1.089% realshow improvement, and extensive ablation studies (RQ1-RQ6)
Strong empirical results consistently outperforming state-of-the-art baselines including generator-evaluator and diffusion-based methods across all metrics
Generalization demonstrated across different reranker backbones (PRM, Pier), retrievers (MF, dual-tower), and improved diversity metrics
High reproducibility standards with detailed implementation details, hyperparameter settings, algorithm description, and promised code release
weaknesses: Theoretical gap: The δₓ term in Eq. (5) is acknowledged as 'not directly optimizable' but the paper provides no empirical analysis of whether it actually becomes small through optimization of other terms. This is a concerning theoretical loose end

Inconsistent online A/B test results (Table 11): while realshow improves (+1.089%), several metrics regress (watch-time -0.091%, share-rate -0.758%, save-rate -0.690%). The explanation about users 'exploring broader videos' is speculative and raises questions about whether the method optimizes for the right objectives

Heuristic generator design choices lack principled justification: Beta distribution selection is motivated only by conjugacy arguments; switching from heuristic to model-based generator at epoch λₑ appears to be a workaround for training instability rather than principled design

Method complexity with three additional hyperparameters (λc, λm, λe) requiring tuning beyond standard ML parameters; sensitivity analysis shows all matter significantly, complicating practical deployment
Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing recent retriever-aware reranker methods and learnable score fusion approaches; most baselines are reranker-only methods

Limited scope analysis: assumes continuous scores in [0,1], unclear how method handles discrete scores or ranking-only retrievers; retriever is fixed during reranker training limiting joint optimization; scalability with candidate pool size not discussed

Moderate novelty: individual components (adversarial learning, noise generation, variational bounds) are standard techniques; main novelty is their combination for reranking and the noise reduction perspective rather than fundamental algorithmic advances

Presentation clarity: heavy notation (x, x', xᵤ, x'ᵤ) can confuse readers; key algorithm details relegated to appendix; 'denoising' framing could be better motivated against alternatives like calibration or distribution matching
